chunks: Ahmad ibn Idris, from Muhammad ibn Ahmad, from Ayyub ibn Nuh, from al-Washsha, from one who mentioned it, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him):

that he considered disreputable the residue of the child of fornication, and the residue of the Jew, and the Christian, and the polytheist, and everyone who opposes Islam; and the most severe of these in his view was the residue of the Nasibi.

key_terms.النَّاصِب: Al-Nasib/Nasibi — one who publicly harbours enmity toward the Ahl al-Bayt of the Prophet; considered among the gravest categories in Shia jurisprudence
key_terms.خَالَفَ الْإِسْلَامَ: Khalafa al-Islam — one who opposes or contradicts Islam; a broad jurisprudential category covering all non-Muslims and deviants
key_terms.سُؤْر: Su'r — the residue or leftover water/drink from which a person has drunk; its ritual status depends on the person who drank from it
key_terms.كَرِهَ: Kariha — to dislike, to deem undesirable; in fiqh, the basis for a ruling of karaha (moral undesirability, makruh)
key_terms.وَلَدُ الزِّنَا: Walad al-zina — child born of fornication/adultery; a specific jurisprudential category

ai.seo_question: What did Imam al-Sadiq say about the ritual status of the drinking residue of a Nasibi and non-Muslims?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (AS) issued a legal ruling declaring the drinking residue (su'r) of certain individuals to be makruh (ritually disreputable), listing the child of adultery, Jews, Christians, polytheists, and all who oppose Islam. Most significantly, the Imam singled out the Nasibi — those who harbour hostility toward the Ahl al-Bayt — as the worst of these categories. This ruling reflects the jurisprudential framework of ritual purity and the spiritual-theological significance of enmity toward the Prophet's household in Shia Islamic law.
word_analysis: the Nasibi (one hostile to the Ahlulbayt)
